blocks.text: Put the application core in the center and talk to everything outside it through ports implemented by adapters.

The core defines **ports**: interfaces for what it offers (inbound) and what it needs (outbound). **Adapters** translate between a port and a technology such as HTTP, SQL or a message broker. Dependencies always point inward, so the core compiles and runs with no framework.

items: **Driving adapters:** call the core (REST, CLI, scheduler).
**Driven adapters:** the core calls them (database, mail, payments).
**Test seam:** replace any adapter with a fake.

blocks.text: The same idea is called Ports and Adapters, Onion or Clean Architecture; the details differ but the inward dependency rule is shared.

walkthrough.note: Three interfaces owned by the core. `RegisterUser` is inbound; `UserStore` and `Mailer` are outbound and describe needs in the core's own words.
The use case implements the inbound port and uses only outbound ports. It imports no framework and no adapter.
Driven adapters implement outbound ports. Here they are in-memory; a JDBC store or SMTP mailer would replace them without touching the core.
Assembly is the only place that sees both sides, choosing which adapters plug into the core.
A driving adapter turns an outside stimulus into a port call. A REST controller or message listener would play this role.

blocks.text: Ride dispatch that must survive swapping map providers.

A dispatch core assigns drivers to riders using ETA and price rules. It asks a `RoutingPort` for travel times and a `DriverLocations` port for positions. One adapter calls a commercial maps API, another replays recorded traffic for tests, a third reads a cache. REST, gRPC and a Kafka listener all drive the same `AssignDriver` port.

lines: interface RoutingPort { Duration eta(Point a, Point b); }

blocks.text: Payoff: changing map vendors or transport protocols never touches dispatch rules, and rules are tested at memory speed.

lists.title: Use when
items: The domain has real rules worth protecting from framework and vendor churn.
Several entry points drive the same use cases: REST, CLI, events.
You want core tests that need no database or network.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: The app is thin CRUD: ports would mirror the framework one to one.
The team is small and the infrastructure will not change.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Ports shaped like the technology (`SqlPort`) instead of the core's needs.
Domain objects annotated with persistence or JSON annotations, quietly coupling the core.
Mapping at every boundary becomes a tax if overdone.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: One interface per class with a single implementation and no second adapter in sight.
Use cases that only forward to one outbound call.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records and sealed interfaces make small, immutable port messages cheap.
Java modules can make adapters depend on the core, never the reverse.

rows.difference: Layering points dependencies down to storage. Hexagonal points them inward and lets the core own the interfaces that infrastructure implements.
Hexagonal applies the Dependency Inversion Principle at architectural scale: the core defines abstractions, outer code depends on them.
Each driven or driving adapter is a GoF Adapter converting between the core's port and an external API.
A repository interface is a typical outbound port, expressed in domain terms and implemented by a persistence adapter.
Injection wires adapters into the core at the composition root, so the core never builds its own adapters.

options.why: Rules sit in a core with ports; transports and providers are adapters you can swap and fake.
Rules would depend on persistence and transport-shaped layers, making swaps and fast tests harder.
MVC separates UI roles; it says nothing about swapping providers or driving the core from events.
A facade simplifies access to a subsystem but doesn't invert dependencies away from vendors.

exercises.prompt: Explain Hexagonal Architecture: what are ports and adapters, and which way do dependencies point?

modelAnswer.text: The application core defines ports, interfaces for what it offers and what it needs. Adapters implement or call those ports for a specific technology, such as HTTP or SQL. Every dependency points inward at the core, which has no framework imports. That inverts the layered style and lets you swap or fake any adapter.

keyPoints: Inbound ports are driven by adapters, outbound ports are implemented by adapters
Core runs and tests without frameworks
Contrast: layered depends toward the database
